5.text: Transformation takes place by the command of the keˊlet, usually at that

6.text: critical age of early youth when shamanistic inspiration first manifests itself.

7.text: It is, however, much dreaded by the youthful adepts; and in most of those

8.text: cases in which I spoke of the young shamans preferring death to obedience

9.text: to the call of the “spirits,” there was connected with the call a reference

10.text: to change of sex. There are, however, various degrees of transformation

12.text: In the first stage, the person subjected to it personates the woman only

13.text: in the manner of braiding and arranging the hair of the head. This usage

14.text: is widespread among the Chukchee, and is adopted not only by shamans at

15.text: the command of the “spirits,” but also by sick persons at the bidding of

16.text: shamans. In the latter case the aim is to change the appearance of the

17.text: patient so as to make him unrecognizable by the “spirits.”

18.text: The second stage is marked by the adoption of female dress, which is

19.text: also practised either for shamanistic or for medico-magical purposes. It does

20.text: not imply complete change of sex. For instance, Kɪˊmɪqäi,¹ who claimed

21.text: for himself shamanistic powers, wore woman’s clothes, which he assumed in

22.text: his early youth. He was afflicted with a strange illness, which caused him to

23.text: sleep in his inner room day after day, almost without interruption. At length

24.text: a keˊlᴇ appeared to him in his sleep and ordered him to put on woman’s

25.text: dress, which he did accordingly. Notwithstanding this, Kɪˊmɪqäi had a wife

26.text: and four children, one of which was still nursing when I saw him. The

27.text: cheeks of Kɪˊmɪqäi were also covered with a stubby black beard, and there

28.text: could be no misunderstanding about the sex to which he really belonged.
